arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Paul Clement argued that Dudenhoeffer recognized a specific pleading standard. He stated that disclosure of negative information can harm the fund. He emphasized the conflict between disclosure and fund value.

Jander's counsel argued that ESOP fiduciaries owe the same duty of prudence. They stated that this duty requires action based on inside information. They argued that delay harms both current holders and potential buyers.
Justice Gorsuch questioned why insider trustees should receive special rules. He asked what employees gain from encouraging such trustees. He noted the possibility of information leaks.

Justice Sotomayor emphasized that both holders and buyers are harmed by delay. She stated that the securities laws do not govern fiduciary duties. She challenged the argument for special treatment of ESOPs.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the pleading standard for ERISA fiduciary duty claims. The core dispute involves whether fiduciaries must disclose negative inside information. IBM claims disclosure would reduce fund value. Jander claims delay harms participants.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: IBM wants the Court to affirm the lower court's application of the Dudenhoeffer standard. IBM argues that disclosing negative information would immediately reduce fund value. IBM seeks to maintain the current pleading requirements for fiduciary claims.

Jander wants the Court to reject the argument that delay is permissible. Jander argues that both current holders and potential buyers suffer from delayed disclosure. Jander seeks a standard that prioritizes participant harm over fund value.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: IBM contends that Dudenhoeffer established a specific pleading standard. This standard acknowledges that insider disclosure can harm the plan. IBM argues that fiduciaries face a conflict between disclosure and fund value.

Jander contends that ESOP fiduciaries owe the same duty of prudence as other ERISA fiduciaries. Jander argues that this duty requires action based on inside information. Jander asserts that delay harms all participants.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Kavanaugh asked if different beneficiary classes create a duty conflict. He questioned whether prudence can be violated when some are harmed and others helped.
Justice Sotomayor asked why the fiduciary duty should not apply. She noted that both holders and buyers are harmed by delay. She distinguished fiduciary duties from securities laws.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the scope of fiduciary duties for employee stock ownership plans. It determines when insiders must disclose negative information. The outcome shapes the balance between fund stability and participant transparency. It sets the standard for future ERISA litigation involving inside information.
